reviews.title: ĐỖ TRẦN LINH TRANG · IELTS 49 · W07 · Đề 1
reviews.overall: Em đã diễn đạt lại đề đúng đại lượng và chia hai đoạn Detail theo nhóm nước có mục đích; các câu về Australia và Thailand có mốc đầu, giữa, cuối. Tuy nhiên, Overview mới nói Thailand tăng chung nên chưa cho thấy nước này đạt đỉnh năm 2006 rồi giảm. Em cũng viết nhiều số bằng dấu chấm thay vì dấu phẩy như trong bảng, và nhận định 245,624 là số thấp nhất toàn bảng dù Argentina chỉ có 235,088 năm 2003. Cô yêu cầu em sửa các chỗ này, bổ sung mốc 2006 của Argentina để thấy khi nào nước này vượt Australia, rồi soát lại toàn bộ số liệu.
reviews.dataGrouping: Em nhóm Argentina và Australia trong Detail 1 để đối chiếu hai xu hướng ngược nhau, rồi dành Detail 2 cho Thailand; cách chia theo đối tượng này phù hợp. Để so sánh có sức thuyết phục hơn, Detail 1 cần thêm hai số của năm 2006 cho Argentina và Australia, vì đó là lúc thứ hạng của hai nước đổi chỗ. Overview cần nói rõ Thailand tăng đến đỉnh 2006 rồi giảm, dù vẫn đứng đầu cả ba năm.

reviews.originalEssay:
The given table  illustrates how many cars were made in three countries: Argentina, Australia and Thailand over a six-year period, commencing from 2003.
Overall, there was an increase in the number of cars produced in Argentina and Thailand, while an opposite trend was observed in Australia. Also of note is that Thailand consistently had the highest figures throughout the years.
To elaborate, in 2003, around 235.088 cars were manufactured in Argentina with a subsequent gradual growth to 466.089 cars in 2009. By contrast, the figure for Australia fell from 452.163 in 2003 to 341.268 in 2006, and then dropped to 245,624 in 2009, which was the lowest figure in the table.
During the same period, the number of cars made in Thailand went up from 735.852 in 2003 to 1.162.356 in 2006, making the highest point of the table. However, the figure declined to 999,963 in 2009, although it remained the highest among the three countries.

reviews.suggestedRevision:
The table compares how many cars were manufactured in Argentina, Australia and Thailand in 2003, 2006 and 2009.

Overall, car production in Argentina rose at each recorded point, whereas Australia's declined throughout. Thailand remained the largest producer in every year; its output peaked in 2006 before falling, although it still ended above its 2003 level.

In 2003, Argentina produced 235,088 cars, fewer than Australia's 452,163. The Argentine figure then increased to 352,759 in 2006, overtaking Australia's 341,268, and reached 466,089 in 2009. By contrast, Australian output continued to fall after 2006 and ended at 245,624 cars, only slightly above Argentina's starting figure.

Thailand followed a different pattern. It made 735,852 cars in 2003, already more than either of the other countries. Production rose substantially to 1,162,356 in 2006, the highest figure in the table. It then declined to 999,963 in 2009, but this was still more than twice Argentina's output in that year.

Overall, there was an increase in the male prison population in a European country between 1911 and 2001. Meanwhile, the figure for female prisoners decreased considerably within the given time frame.
To elaborate, in 1911, there were around 18,000 male prisoners. The figure remained relatively stable from 1911 to 1971. However, the figure showed a dramatic upward trend to about 45,000 in 2001, making it the highest point of the prison population in a European country from 1911 to 2001.
Regarding the category with female data, the prison population went down considerably from just over 3,000 in 1911 to nearly 500 in 1941, the lowest figure on the chart. However, the figure showed an increase with some fluctuations to around 2,000 in 2001.

The two line charts show how many men and women were in prison in a European country from 1911 to 2001.

Overall, men outnumbered women in every year shown. The male total initially fell before recovering and rising sharply near the end of the period, especially between 1971 and 1981. By contrast, the female total dropped to a low in 1941 and then fluctuated, finishing below its starting level.

In 1911, there were approximately 18,000 male prisoners, and this figure was similar in 1921. It fell to about 10,000 in 1931 before returning to nearly 20,000 by 1951. After remaining close to that level until 1971, the number jumped to around 39,000 in 1981 and climbed further to roughly 46,000 in 2001.

The number of female prisoners began at just over 3,000 in 1911 and declined to around 500 in 1941. It then rose to approximately 1,500 in 1961, before falling again to roughly 700 in 1971. From there, the figure increased to about 1,900 by 2001, still far below the male figure in the same year.

reviews.originalEssay:
The given line chart illustrates the consumption of fish and four different kinds of meat in a European country over a 25-year period, commencing from 1979.
Overall, there was an increase in the use of chicken in a European country from 1979 to 2004, while an opposite trend was observed in the case of beef, lamb and fish. Also of note is that fish consistently had the lowest figures throughout the years.
To elaborate, in 1979, about 140 grams of chicken were eaten with a subsequent rise to 200 grams in 1989, making chicken the most popular meat from that time onwards, and the consumption of chicken went up to 250 grams in 2004. The figures for beef started at around 220 grams, the highest figure in 1979, after which they fluctuated considerably between 1979 and 1989 before dropping dramatically to about 110 grams in 2004.
Regarding categories with lower data, in 1979, 150 grams of lamb decreased significantly to just over 50 grams in 2004. The figures for fish also declined from 60 grams to almost 35 grams during the same time, which was the lowest figure over the whole timescale.

Overall, there was a stable period in the share of young people in higher education in country B, while the percentages increased in the other countries. Also of note is that country D consistently had the highest figures throughout the years.

The given line chart illustrates the proportion of female members of parliament in five European countries over a 12-year period, commencing from 2000.
Overall, there was an increase in the percentage of female parliamentarians in all five countries, with the UK witnessing the most pronounced rise. Despite this, the UK had the lowest figure from 2000 to 2008, and Belgium joined in 2012.
To elaborate, the share of female parliamentarians in Germany grew gradually from around 34% in 2000 to 35% in 2008, reaching its peak that year, before rising to about 37% in 2012. The figure for Italy, likewise, went up from just over 26% in 2000 to 39% in 2012, reaching the highest point of the whole chart. The figure for France also increased from 25% in 2000 to nearly 37% in 2004, the top ranking of the year, after which it dropped to 28% in 2008 before growing to upward of 31% in 2012.
Regarding the remaining, in 2000, 17% of members of parliament in Belgium was reported as female. This figure rose to 28% in 2012. The figure for the UK went up substantially by around 24% over the whole timeline.
